column4: Feeding the needy, orphan, and captive is the concrete deed whose disavowal of human payment follows in 76:9 and whose divine wage appears in 76:12 and 76:22.
God recompenses their patience with a garden and silk, explicitly making the garden hospitality that culminates in 76:22 a wage.
Silver vessels and cups circulate among the garden people, supplying the particular hospitality immediately before their striving is pronounced thanked in 76:22.
The silver vessels are precisely measured, adding measured provision to the garden scene whose guests' effort receives acknowledgment in 76:22.
The Lord clothes the garden people and gives them a pure drink; this is the last concrete gift before 76:22 identifies the whole reception as their wage.
One who wants the immediate life receives only the allotted portion God wills and then Hell, the deliberately failed counterpart to the afterlife striving in 17:19.
The great overwhelming event arrives, naming the event at which 79:35 says each person remembers their striving.
Hell is exposed to everyone who can see immediately after remembered striving, turning the review of work into a visible outcome.
The transgressor opens the failed branch of the reckoning that follows the recollection of striving in 79:35.
Preferring the nearer life identifies the aim of the failed worker whose destination 79:39 states.
Hell is the abode of the one who preferred worldly life, completing the negative wage of 79:37-38.
Fearing the Lord's station and restraining desire identify the contrary labor whose destination follows in 79:41.
The garden is the abode of the self-restraining person, completing the successful wage after striving is remembered.
No bearer bears another's burden; just before the rule about striving, this makes each labor account personally nontransferable.
The final destination is to the Lord, completing the effort-and-recompense sequence of 53:39-41 with the owner of the account.
Hell is named as the recompense of those whose striving was lost and whose deeds had no weight in 18:104-105.
A fiercely hot fire identifies the abyss reached by the person with light scales, completing that failed account's destination.
Giving and guarding oneself begin the successful form of the diverse striving announced in 92:4.
Affirming the best promise supplies the conviction that directs the giver's effort toward its favorable result.
God eases the giver toward ease, making rightly aimed striving issue in a fitting path and outcome.
Withholding and deeming oneself self-sufficient, ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ, begin the failed branch of striving and expose false sufficiency as its motive.
Denying the best promise supplies the orientation that makes the miser's effort fail.
God eases the miser toward hardship, giving the second form of diverse striving its contrary result.
Each person's record is fastened to them and brought out as an open book, concretely attaching the account to its worker.
The person is told to read their own record and is sufficient that day as an accountant against themself, joining self-inspection, sufficiency, and reckoning.
Receiving the book in the right hand identifies the favorable account holder before 84:8 states that his reckoning is easy.
Receiving the book behind the back identifies the failed account holder before his call for destruction in 84:11.
His former joy among his family contrasts with the lasting joy after an easy account and explains the false expectation of no return in 84:14.
Everyone has ranks according to what they did, so differing labor receives a differentiated outcome under God's complete awareness.
No deed escapes God's witness, not even an atom's weight, and everything is in a clear record; this is exhaustive labor accounting.
God has encompassed people and counted them exactly, a direct formulation of the section's counting sense of account.
Each person comes to God individually, showing the personal presentation produced by the exact count in 19:94.
Even a mustard-seed weight hidden in rock, heaven, or earth is brought by God, showing that no minute work can escape the account.
Not an atom's weight or anything smaller or greater escapes God; all is in a clear record, specifying the precision of final counting.
A record speaks truth and no one is wronged, while obligation stays within capacity; the account measures real work without manufacturing impossible liability.
Every expenditure and journey is written as a righteous deed so God may reward the best of their work, continuing 9:120's accounting of fatigue itself.
Those in lasting punishment are asked whether they are being recompensed for anything but what they earned, identifying torment as settled acquisition.
Faces are cast into the fire and asked whether they are repaid except for what they did, visibly joining deed, wage, and punished face.
On that day no soul is wronged and people are recompensed only for what they did, stating the exact labor settlement.
The condemned are recompensed only for what they used to do, defining punishment as the corresponding wage of action.
Disbelievers are told not to excuse themselves that day because they are repaid only for what they did, making the account answer deed rather than plea.
Righteous work benefits its doer and evil works against its doer, while the Lord wrongs no servant; action returns to its source justly.
Whoever works righteousness does so for themself and whoever does evil works against themself, before all return to the Lord.
Doing good benefits the doer and doing evil harms the doer, expressing the return of labor upon its worker.
Every soul earns only against itself and no bearer carries another's burden before return to God, defining the account's personal ownership.
Each soul receives the good it earns and bears the evil it earns, a compact two-sided ledger of acquisition.
On Resurrection Day every soul is fully paid what it earned without wrong, another exact formulation of completed wages.
Whoever does evil is recompensed for it and finds no protector against God, preventing harmful work from escaping settlement.
Believing righteous workers enter the garden without even a speck of wrong, supplying the favorable side of 4:123's deed account.
The Lord will fully repay everyone for their deeds and is informed of what they do, joining complete knowledge to full payment.
Whatever good people spend is fully repaid to them without wrong, making voluntary expenditure an action with an exact return.
Whatever is spent in God's path is fully repaid without injustice, another explicit conversion of purposeful outlay into undiminished wage.
Those who deny God's signs have their works nullified and are asked whether they are recompensed except for what they did.
Those who turn back from faith lose their deeds in both worlds and remain in the Fire, making sustained work end without profitable share.
Their works fail in this world and the Hereafter and no helpers remain, a repeated formulation of labor stripped of every return.
Rejecting faith makes work collapse and leaves the person among afterlife losers, linking null labor to final loss.
The idolaters' works collapse and they remain in the Fire, a direct pairing of wasted activity with its failed wage.
They enjoyed their allotted share as earlier peoples did, but their works collapsed; temporary portion and final loss meet in one reckoning.
Because they hated what God sent down, He made their works collapse; rejection removes the hoped-for return of labor.
Following what angers God and disliking His pleasure causes works to collapse, tying divine رضا and the survival of deeds together.
Their spending resembles a freezing wind that destroys a wrongdoer's crop, a concrete agricultural image of expended labor losing its yield.
A treasured garden burns when its owner is old and dependents are weak, dramatizing the ruin of an expected yield precisely when its wage is needed.
The faithful rejoice that God does not waste the believers' wage, directly affirming preservation of earned return.
Those who hold to the Book and establish prayer learn that God does not waste the wage of reformers.
Patience is commanded because God does not waste the wage of doers of good, setting endurance against fruitless weariness.
Joseph is established in the land and the verse states that God does not waste the wage of doers of good, showing preserved labor in worldly placement.
Joseph says that reverence and patience are not lost because God does not waste the wage of doers of good, explaining his satisfaction after long trial.
God asks whether those who submit could be made like criminals, rejecting a reckoning that gives opposed workers the same wage.
“What is wrong with you; how do you judge?” exposes the faulty calculation behind the impossible equality posed in 68:35.
Solomon is told that God's gift may be bestowed or withheld without account, placing sovereign abundance beyond the finite counting applied to human work.
The hoarder calculates that wealth has made him immortal; the following fire corrects a false estimate of wealth's sufficiency and lasting wage.
God extends His gift to both the immediate-life seeker and the afterlife striver, clarifying that present provision alone is not the final labor verdict.
Worldly preferences differ, but the Hereafter has greater ranks and preference; this explains the larger return of the striving in 17:19.
The verse points to what is in Moses' scrolls, locating the labor-account rule of 53:39 in the source tradition named by the section.
Abraham who fulfilled is named beside Moses, completing the scriptural attribution that frames the rules in 53:38-41.
God says guidance rests upon Him in the same passage that separates diverse strivings and their outcomes.
The first life and the Hereafter belong to God, grounding His authority over both the labor period and its final wage.
God says He is counting for the rejecters a count, a non-ḥisāb formulation of the deliberate divine enumeration developed in the section.
God encompasses what His messengers carry and counts everything numerically, extending divine counting to exhaustive knowledge.
Seeking God's pleasure is set against incurring His wrath, so رضا marks a decisive difference in the final valuation of action.
The two groups have differing degrees with God, giving the opposed relation to divine pleasure in 3:162 a measured outcome.
Gardens and lasting dwellings are promised, but God's pleasure is declared greater, ranking رضا above even the visible wage.
God is pleased with the believers' pledged intention and rewards them with a near victory, a historical instance of divine رضا becoming recompense.
The faithful seek bounty and divine pleasure, and righteous workers among them are promised forgiveness and a great wage.
The question whether believers calculate they will enter the garden before severe trial challenges an account that expects reward without tested effort.
The question whether people calculate they will enter the garden before their striving and patience are disclosed links hoped-for reward to proven labor.
